The '''Lyapunov–Malkin theorem''' (named for [[Aleksandr Mikhailovich Lyapunov|Aleksandr Lyapunov]] and {{ill|Ioel Malkin|ru|Малкин, Иоэль Гильевич}}) is a mathematical theorem detailing stability of nonlinear systems.<ref name="Zenkov">{{cite journal |last=Zenkov |first=D. V. |last2=Bloch |first2=A. M. |last3=Marsden |first3=J. E. |year=2002 |title=Lyapunov–Malkin Theorem and Stabilization of the Unicycle Rider |journal=Systems and Control Letters |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=293–302 |doi=10.1016/S0167-6911(01)00187-6 |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/20025/1/ZeBlMa2002.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Nonholonomic mechanics and control|date=2015|last=Bloch |first=Anthony |author2=Krishnaprasad, Perinkulam Sambamurthy |author3=Murray, R. M. |isbn=9781493930173|edition=2nd |location=New York, NY|oclc=932167031}}</ref>

==Theorem==
In the system of [[differential equation]]s,

:<math>\dot x = Ax + X(x,y),\quad\dot y = Y(x,y)</math>

where <math>x \in \mathbb{R}^m</math> and <math>y \in \mathbb{R}^n</math> are components of the system state, <math>A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times m}</math> is a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] that represents the linear dynamics of <math>x</math>, and <math>X : \mathbb{R}^m\times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m</math> and <math>Y : \mathbb{R}^m\times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n</math> represent higher-order nonlinear terms. If all [[eigenvalue]]s of the matrix <math>A</math> have negative real parts, and ''X''(''x'',&nbsp;''y''), ''Y''(''x'',&nbsp;''y'') vanish when ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, then the solution ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 of this system is stable with respect to (''x'',&nbsp;''y'') and asymptotically stable with respect to ''x''. If a solution (''x''(''t''),&nbsp;''y''(''t'')) is close enough to the solution ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, then

:<math>\lim_{t \to \infty}x(t) = 0,\quad \lim_{t \to \infty}y(t) = c.</math>

== Example ==
Consider the vector field given by 

<math>\dot x = -x + x^2y,
\quad\dot y = xy^2</math>

In this case, ''A'' = -1 and ''X''(0,&nbsp;''y'') = ''Y''(0,&nbsp;''y'') = 0 for all ''y'', so this system satisfy the hypothesis of Lyapunov-Malkin theorem. 

The figure below shows a plot of this vector field along with some trajectories that pass near (0,0). As expected by the theorem, it can be seen that trajectories in the neighborhood of (0,0) converges to a point in the form (0,''c'').
